about: Fact cards: a reviewed fact over muted footage. Pick footage and approve in: node scripts/review.mjs. Only status 'approved' with footage goes live.

items.title: You are being rebuilt right now
items.text: Your body makes about 2.4 million new red blood cells every second.

items.title: Made of starlight
items.text: The Big Bang made only the lightest elements. The carbon, oxygen and iron in you were forged later, inside stars.

items.title: If the universe were one year old
items.text: Squeeze the universe's whole history into one calendar year, and the time since the last ice age fits into the final 23 seconds of December 31st.

items.title: Old light
items.text: The sunlight on your skin left the Sun about 8 minutes ago.

items.title: More trees than stars
items.text: Earth has about three trillion trees: more than the 100 to 400 billion stars in the whole Milky Way.

items.title: Three hearts
items.text: An octopus has three hearts, and its blood carries oxygen with a copper-rich protein instead of iron.

items.title: Directions, by dance
items.text: A honey bee that finds flowers dances back at the hive, and the angle and length of her waggle tell the others which way to fly and how far.

items.title: Why six arms?
items.text: Snowflakes tend toward six-fold symmetry because ice itself is built as a hexagonal crystal.

items.title: The Moon is slowly leaving
items.text: Lasers bounced off mirrors left on the Moon show it moving about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year.

items.title: Hearing space ripple
items.text: On 14 September 2015, detectors on Earth first caught ripples in spacetime itself, from two black holes merging about 1.4 billion light-years away.

cite.title: Wikipedia: First observation of gravitational waves

items.title: Thinking is hungry work
items.text: Your brain is about 2% of your body weight, yet it uses up to 20% of your body's energy.

items.title: Still growing
items.text: A Great Basin bristlecone pine in California called Methuselah is more than 4,800 years old.

items.title: The softest coat
items.text: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal: up to 150,000 hairs in every square centimetre.

items.title: Half a rainbow
items.text: From the ground a rainbow looks like an arc, but from a plane, with enough mist below, you can see it as a full circle.

items.title: A crowded teaspoon
items.text: A single teaspoon of productive soil can hold anywhere from 100 million to 3 billion bacteria.

items.title: Two summers a year
items.text: Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, seeing two summers. Birds from Iceland and Greenland average about 70,900 km a round trip.

items.title: A coat that grows a garden
items.text: A sloth's grooved hair hosts green algae, which tint its coat to blend into the trees.

items.title: Regrowing what's lost
items.text: Axolotls can regrow whole limbs, gills, and even parts of their eyes and brain.

items.title: A map in the magnetic field
items.text: Sea turtles find their way across open ocean using Earth's magnetic field. Some females come back to nest on the very beach where they hatched.

items.title: Who's that in the mirror?
items.text: Elephants recognise themselves in a mirror, a sign of self-awareness shown by only a few animals, including some apes and dolphins.

items.title: Toolmakers
items.text: New Caledonian crows make their own tools, and can even shape twigs into hooks.

items.note: Pixabay 'mantis shrimp' returns sushi and cooking clips; use photos or Commons.
items.title: Colours we can't imagine
items.text: Our eyes have four types of light-sensing cell. A mantis shrimp's have between 12 and 16.

items.title: Songs that change
items.text: Male humpback whales sing complex songs up to half an hour long, and when one changes his song, others nearby pick up the change.

items.note: No Pixabay video; photos and Commons only.
items.title: The longest flight
items.text: Bar-tailed godwits fly from Alaska to New Zealand across the Pacific without stopping: the longest known non-stop flight of any bird.

items.title: Frozen, then fine
items.text: Wood frogs survive winter with 65 to 70% of their body water frozen, using glucose as a natural antifreeze.

items.title: Sleeping with one eye open
items.text: Dolphins can sleep with one half of the brain at a time, keeping the other half alert, and the eye on the sleeping side closed.

items.title: Fireflies in sync
items.text: Each June in the Great Smoky Mountains, one firefly species flashes in unison, sending waves of light and dark through the forest.

items.title: A forest that is one tree
items.text: Pando, in Utah, looks like a grove of about 47,000 aspens. They're all one tree, connected by a single root system.

items.title: The shy plant
items.text: Touch a sensitive plant and its leaves fold inward and droop, then open again a few minutes later.

items.title: Watch it grow
items.text: Some bamboo can grow 91 cm in a single day: about a millimetre every 90 seconds.

items.title: Two leaves, a thousand years
items.text: Welwitschia grows just two leaves in its whole life, and some plants are thousands of years old. In Afrikaans its name means 'two leaves, can't die'.

items.title: The biggest tree
items.text: General Sherman, a giant sequoia in California, is the largest known living single-stem tree on Earth by volume.

items.title: Riding a ring of air
items.text: A dandelion seed's fluffy parachute creates a special ring of swirling air that stays attached above it, carrying it far on the wind.

items.title: A 2,000-year-old seed
items.text: In 2005, scientists sprouted a 2,000-year-old date palm seed: the oldest seed ever germinated with human help.

items.title: The biggest flower
items.text: Rafflesia arnoldii produces the largest individual flower on Earth.

items.title: Roots holding hands with fungi
items.text: About 70% of plant species partner with fungi whose threads grow right into their roots, trading sugar for water and nutrients.

items.title: Self-cleaning leaves
items.text: Water beads up on a lotus leaf and rolls off, picking up dirt as it goes, thanks to a microscopic surface texture.

items.title: The tallest tree
items.text: Hyperion, a coast redwood in California, is the tallest known living tree: 116.22 metres when measured in 2026.
